title: Esi and the Elephant’s Secret Path

pages.text: Eight-year-old Esi lived in a village near Mole National Park in northern Ghana. One morning after the rain, she found a line of giant round footprints pressed into the red mud near the edge of her family’s farm. Each footprint was as wide as a cooking pot!
sentences: Eight-year-old Esi lived in a village near Mole National Park in northern Ghana.
One morning after the rain, she found a line of giant round footprints pressed into the red mud near the edge of her family’s farm.
Each footprint was as wide as a cooking pot!
pages.alt: Eight-year-old Esi kneels beside a row of huge round elephant footprints in the damp red earth near Mole National Park.

pages.text: Ranger Braimah arrived on his bicycle in his green ranger uniform. ‘Good morning, Esi!’ he smiled. ‘An elephant family walked past here before dawn. Look how the big footprints and little footprints stay close together. They are following an ancient elephant path that leads from the river to the fruiting shea trees.’
sentences: Ranger Braimah arrived on his bicycle in his green ranger uniform.
‘Good morning, Esi!’ he smiled.
‘An elephant family walked past here before dawn.
Look how the big footprints and little footprints stay close together.
They are following an ancient elephant path that leads from the river to the fruiting shea trees.’
pages.alt: Ranger Braimah in his green uniform points along the trail of large and small elephant footprints while Esi listens.

pages.text: From a high wooden viewing platform inside the park boundary, Ranger Braimah handed Esi a pair of binoculars. ‘Always stay quiet, downwind, and far back in a safe place with a ranger,’ he reminded her. Down by the waterhole stood six grey African elephants, led by the biggest female with long curved ears.
sentences: From a high wooden viewing platform inside the park boundary, Ranger Braimah handed Esi a pair of binoculars.
‘Always stay quiet, downwind, and far back in a safe place with a ranger,’ he reminded her.
Down by the waterhole stood six grey African elephants, led by the biggest female with long curved ears.
pages.alt: From a high wooden platform, Esi looks through binoculars at a family of six elephants by a sunny waterhole.

pages.text: ‘Who is the leader in the front?’ whispered Esi. ‘She is the matriarch, the oldest and wisest grandmother of the family,’ said Ranger Braimah. ‘Male elephants leave the herd when they grow up, but mothers, sisters and calves stay together. The matriarch can remember where to find water during dry years, even a place she visited thirty years ago!’
sentences: ‘Who is the leader in the front?’ whispered Esi.
‘She is the matriarch, the oldest and wisest grandmother of the family,’ said Ranger Braimah.
‘Male elephants leave the herd when they grow up, but mothers, sisters and calves stay together.
The matriarch can remember where to find water during dry years, even a place she visited thirty years ago!’
pages.alt: The wise grandmother elephant leads the herd and a tiny calf along the waterhole edge while flapping her large ears.

pages.text: Esi watched the elephants flap their huge ears and spray cool mud onto their backs with their trunks. ‘Why do they flap their ears and wear mud?’ she asked. ‘An elephant’s ears are full of blood vessels,’ said Ranger Braimah. ‘Flapping them cools the blood like a fan, and wet mud acts like sunscreen to protect their skin from heat and insects!’
sentences: Esi watched the elephants flap their huge ears and spray cool mud onto their backs with their trunks.
‘Why do they flap their ears and wear mud?’ she asked.
‘An elephant’s ears are full of blood vessels,’ said Ranger Braimah.
‘Flapping them cools the blood like a fan, and wet mud acts like sunscreen to protect their skin from heat and insects!’
pages.alt: An elephant sprays cool mud over its back with its trunk while flapping its wide ears.

pages.text: Suddenly, all six elephants froze. The matriarch lifted her trunk and pressed one big front foot flat against the ground. Yet Esi heard nothing at all! Seconds later, another elephant family appeared from behind the distant baobab trees and walked straight toward them, touching trunks in a friendly greeting.
sentences: Suddenly, all six elephants froze.
The matriarch lifted her trunk and pressed one big front foot flat against the ground.
Yet Esi heard nothing at all!
Seconds later, another elephant family appeared from behind the distant baobab trees and walked straight toward them, touching trunks in a friendly greeting.
pages.alt: The matriarch elephant stands very still with one foot pressed to the ground while another elephant group approaches from the baobab trees.

pages.text: ‘How did they know the other elephants were coming when there was no sound?’ asked Esi. Ranger Braimah smiled. ‘Elephants make deep rumbles called infrasound that are too low for human ears to hear! Those low vibrations travel for kilometres through the air and through the ground, and elephants feel them through the soft pads of their feet.’
sentences: ‘How did they know the other elephants were coming when there was no sound?’ asked Esi.
Ranger Braimah smiled.
‘Elephants make deep rumbles called infrasound that are too low for human ears to hear!
Those low vibrations travel for kilometres through the air and through the ground, and elephants feel them through the soft pads of their feet.’
pages.alt: Ranger Braimah taps the wooden railing gently while Esi places her hand flat on the wood to feel the vibration.

pages.text: Walking back toward the village farms, Esi saw her mother hanging wooden beehives along a wire fence between posts around their maize field. ‘Mama, why are we putting beehives by the farm?’ Esi asked. ‘To protect both our crops and the elephants,’ said Mama. ‘Elephants are afraid of honeybees stinging the sensitive skin inside their trunks!’
sentences: Walking back toward the village farms, Esi saw her mother hanging wooden beehives along a wire fence between posts around their maize field.
‘Mama, why are we putting beehives by the farm?’ Esi asked.
‘To protect both our crops and the elephants,’ said Mama.
‘Elephants are afraid of honeybees stinging the sensitive skin inside their trunks!’
pages.alt: Esi’s mother hangs wooden beehives on a wire fence along the edge of a green maize farm while Esi and Ranger Braimah watch.

pages.text: ‘When an elephant touches the wire, the hives swing and the bees buzz out,’ said Ranger Braimah. ‘The elephant turns back safely to its forest corridor, and your family harvests both maize and sweet honey!’ Esi smiled at the big footprints in the soil. Now she knew how science helps people and giant neighbours share the land in peace. The end.

pages.alt: Esi, Mama and Ranger Braimah smile together beside the beehive fence as elephants walk peacefully along the distant park path at sunset.

activities.question: Who leads an African elephant family herd and remembers where to find water?
options: The matriarch, the oldest and wisest grandmother elephant
A tall giraffe that walks in front
The fastest bird in the trees
activities.explanation: Elephant herds are matriarchal: the oldest female (the matriarch) leads the family and remembers waterholes and migration paths.

activities.question: Why do elephants flap their big ears and spray mud on their skin?
options: To cool their blood and protect their skin from heat and insects
To help them fly over rivers
To make their ears grow longer
activities.explanation: Blood vessels in an elephant’s large ears release heat when flapped, and mud acts like a cooling sunscreen.

activities.definition: Deep sound vibrations that are too low for human ears to hear.
distractors: A very high whistle that only birds make
A bright flash of light in the sky

activities.question: How does a beehive fence help both farmers and elephants near Mole National Park?
options: Bees safely turn elephants away from crops, and farmers harvest honey
The bees carry the maize into the barn
Elephants eat the wooden beehives instead of corn
The fence traps elephants inside the farm
activities.explanation: Elephants avoid buzzing honeybees around their sensitive trunks, so beehive fences protect crops peacefully while providing honey.

activities.prompt: Why is it important to leave safe walking corridors between farms so elephants can reach rivers and trees?
Put Esi’s discoveries in the right order.
items: Esi finds giant round elephant footprints near the edge of the farm.
From a safe platform, Esi watches the matriarch lead her herd.
Ranger Braimah explains how elephants send low rumbles in the ground.
Mama shows how beehive fences protect the maize farm peacefully.

activities.prompt: How do you feel when people find a kind, clever way to solve a problem without hurting wildlife?

glossary.definition: The oldest and wisest female elephant who leads a family herd.
Very low-pitched sound vibrations below the range of human hearing.
Tiny, rapid back-and-forth movements that travel through air, water or solid ground.
A safe natural pathway that wildlife use to travel between habitats.
